people.name: Anna
people.whatWeWillDo: Aperitivo on the Navigli like we do it, not like the guidebook, then a walk through the old ringhiera courtyards of Isola, and if you want, risotto at mine. Next I am off to Helsinki for Slush, on my own: I would love a real sauna, whatever locals do this time of year, and a chat over coffee with other travellers and families who share my weakness for Lego and football.
people.whyIHost: I moved here from Bergamo ten years ago and somebody showed me the real Milano. I work at a startup and travel a lot for it, and the best trips were always the ones where someone local opened the door. Now it is my turn.
people.languages: Italian, English, a bit of German

people.name: Davide
people.whatWeWillDo: Breakfast at the bar under my flat in NoLo, the Saturday market on Viale Papiniano, then the Monumentale cemetery, which sounds strange and is the most beautiful open-air museum in the city. We get everywhere by tram: I know every line by heart.
people.whyIHost: I drove trams in Milano for twenty-two years and watched visitors get lost every single day. Now I am retired and I finally have the time to show them the way.

people.name: Chiara
people.whatWeWillDo: Live music in a basement club in Porta Venezia, a late cotoletta, then the Darsena at midnight when it finally goes quiet. I have a small guest room in Città Studi if you need a bed for a night or two.
people.whyIHost: I mix sound for concerts and spend half the year on the road with bands. People have put me up in every city I can think of, so my spare room is the least I can give back.

people.name: Julien
people.whatWeWillDo: Focaccia hunter on a slow train trip through the north, ten days in Milano now. I like the places that are not on Instagram, a good bookshop and a bar where people argue about politics.

people.name: Tom
people.whatWeWillDo: Walking down from Lake Como along the canals, then a fortnight in Milano with sore feet. Keen on proper food, old bookshops and anyone happy to explain the football to me.

people.name: Lucía
people.whatWeWillDo: I travel slow, one month in Italy and ten days of it in Milano. I love to cook, so markets and home kitchens are my favourite thing, and I can teach you a real gazpacho in exchange for your risotto.

people.name: Aino
people.whatWeWillDo: An evening at a public sauna on the shore: wood-fired heat, then down the ladder into the sea, yes, even in the dark season, then back into the steam. After, salmon soup and a cinnamon bun at a café I trust.
people.whyIHost: Sauna is where Finns actually talk. I love watching visitors go from terrified of the cold water to asking when we can go again.

people.name: Mikko
people.whatWeWillDo: Smoked fish at the old market hall by the harbour, a walk on the island fortress while the light goes at three, then the lights along the Esplanadi. If there is a home game we finish at the hockey or the football: the noise alone is worth the trip.
people.whyIHost: The dark season has a bad name, even with Finns. I think it is when Helsinki is most itself, with a candle in every window, and I like proving it to people.

people.name: Laura
people.whatWeWillDo: A Saturday morning at our boys' football club (they are 8 and 10), then pancakes at home and a Lego session that always runs longer than planned. Antti looks after the sauna, I look after the coffee.
people.whyIHost: We moved back to Helsinki from Rotterdam when the boys were small and missed having friends from everywhere. Hosting other families gives them that again, and gives us an excuse to explore our own city.

people.name: Antti
people.whatWeWillDo: Our family sauna on a Sunday evening, the outdoor ice rink if it is cold enough, and the big library downtown where kids can build and play for free. Laura says I talk too much about football, and our two boys, 8 and 10, agree with her.
people.whyIHost: I coach the under-10 team our older son plays in, and I like meeting parents from other countries on the touchline. The kids never need a common language, only a ball.

people.name: Marta
people.whatWeWillDo: Our first real cold-weather trip, a week in Helsinki with our boys, 7 and 9. They want snow, Lego and a football match, in that order; I want a sauna and one evening of grown-up conversation. Pablo has already packed too many jumpers.

people.name: Pablo
people.whatWeWillDo: Marta planned the trip; my job is keeping two football-mad boys, 7 and 9, warm and fed. We would love to meet a local family, swap Lego for an afternoon and learn what Finnish kids do when it is dark at four.

people.name: Lena
people.whatWeWillDo: In Helsinki for Slush, pitching our climate-data startup, so my days are fully booked. The evenings are free and I would rather spend them where locals go than at one more afterparty.

people.name: Oliver
people.whatWeWillDo: Recently retired from teaching geography, finally seeing the places I drew on the board. A week in Helsinki this time of year, then the ferry to Stockholm: markets, long walks whatever the weather, and anyone willing to explain the rules of ice hockey.

people.name: Graziella
people.whatWeWillDo: The Sant'Ambrogio market early, when the stallholders still have time to talk, then ribollita in my kitchen with greens from my own plot. If your legs are good, we take the bus up to Fiesole and look down at the whole city, with the Duomo in the middle.
people.whyIHost: I was born in San Frediano and never saw a reason to leave. My grandchildren have grown up and moved away, so now I cook for whoever knocks.

people.name: Lorenzo
people.whatWeWillDo: Sunset from Piazzale Michelangelo, then down the steps to Santo Spirito, where half the city sits on the church steps with a drink. I study restoration, so if you like I show you the Oltrarno workshops where they still gild frames and bind books by hand.
people.whyIHost: Florence can feel like a museum with a queue. I grew up here and I like showing people the part that is still a neighbourhood, with football in the piazza and grandmothers on the benches.

people.name: Rosanna
people.whatWeWillDo: Testaccio market in the morning, where we buy what we cook for lunch: cacio e pepe, artichokes if they are in season, and a long table with whoever is around. In the afternoon we walk up the Aventine and peek through the famous keyhole at St Peter's dome.
people.whyIHost: For years I taught cooking to tourists who never saw a real Roman kitchen. Now I prefer to open my own, with the radio on and the neighbours shouting across the courtyard.

people.name: Samuel
people.whatWeWillDo: Pigneto on a Friday night, when the street fills up and nobody is in a hurry, then a supplì on the way home. On Sunday morning we take bikes along the Via Appia Antica, past tombs two thousand years old, and stop for a picnic under the pines.
people.whyIHost: I grew up as the one who showed Rome to the cousins visiting from abroad, and somewhere along the way it became my favourite thing to do.

people.name: Elsa
people.whatWeWillDo: Fika in Gamla stan, coffee and a cardamom bun in a cellar café, then a walk along the water to Södermalm for the view back over the old town. If the lakes freeze hard enough, I lend you skates and we go out on the ice like everyone else.
people.whyIHost: I moved here from a small town up north to study and fell for the city in my first dark season. Showing it to newcomers reminds me why.

people.name: Lars
people.whatWeWillDo: We take a commuter boat out into the archipelago and walk round an island where you hear nothing but the water. Back in town, the Vasa museum, a warship that sank on her first voyage and came up more than three hundred years later, and meatballs at mine.
people.whyIHost: I was an engineer on the archipelago boats for twenty-five years and I still think they are the best way to see the city. My wife says I have found a new audience for the same stories.

people.name: Aminata
people.whatWeWillDo: A picnic by the Canal Saint-Martin, then up through Belleville, where I live, to the top of the park for the view over the rooftops. On Sunday I take you to the market on my street, the loudest in Paris, and we cook whatever we found.
people.whyIHost: I am a nurse and I work nights, so my free days fall at odd times and I spend them walking. Paris is kinder than its reputation once somebody shows you where to sit down.

people.name: Bernard
people.whatWeWillDo: The bookstalls along the Seine, where I know which sellers still keep the good old editions, then a slow lap of the Jardin du Luxembourg to watch the chess players. If you are curious, I show you how a book is sewn and bound by hand.
people.whyIHost: I bound books for forty years in the Latin Quarter. Now I am retired, my wife has her choir, and I have all the time in the world to walk.

people.name: Grace
people.whatWeWillDo: Brixton Village for food from half the world, then a pub quiz where my team has never once won. On a clear day we walk up through Greenwich Park and look down the river at the whole city, from the old naval college to the towers.
people.whyIHost: I was born in south London and I get defensive when visitors only see the museums. The city is best from the top deck of a bus, on the way to somebody's kitchen.

people.name: Colin
people.whatWeWillDo: A Sunday walk across Hampstead Heath to Parliament Hill, where the whole skyline lines up, then a roast in a pub with a fire. If you are brave, the ponds on the Heath are open all year and the regulars swim whatever the weather.
people.whyIHost: I walk the Thames Path end to end every few years and still find streets I have never seen. London is too big to know alone, so I like sharing the bits I have found.

people.name: Jonas
people.whatWeWillDo: The Tempelhof field, the old airport where we walk or cycle down the runway, then the Grunewald forest if you want trees instead of concrete. Evenings, a beer from the Späti on the canal bank and wherever the night goes from there.
people.whyIHost: I grew up in a village in Brandenburg and came to Berlin at nineteen with one bag. Friends showed me how to live here; now I do the same for others.

people.name: Ingrid
people.whatWeWillDo: Mauerpark on a Sunday: the flea market, and the karaoke in the amphitheatre if the weather allows. Then I show you where the Wall ran past my street, and we finish with coffee and cake at my kitchen table in Prenzlauer Berg.
people.whyIHost: I grew up in East Berlin and was twenty-eight when the Wall came down. I like telling visitors what it was like, before the city forgets.

people.name: Pilar
people.whatWeWillDo: El Rastro on a Sunday morning, then a vermouth in La Latina, standing at the bar like a real madrileña. In the afternoon a rowing boat on the lake in the Retiro, and dinner late, because that is how we do it here.
people.whyIHost: For years I rented my spare room to students and I missed every one of them when they left. Hosting travellers keeps the house full of languages.

people.name: Miguel
people.whatWeWillDo: A long lunch in Malasaña, the Templo de Debod for sunset, and churros with chocolate when the night is over. If there is a match on, you watch it with my friends: in Madrid you pick a side, and you pick it fast.
people.whyIHost: My parents came from Manila and I grew up between two kitchens in Madrid. I like showing visitors that the city is bigger than the Prado and the Gran Vía.

people.name: Tomáš
people.whatWeWillDo: Charles Bridge at dawn, before the crowds, with a camera if you like photography. Then up to Vyšehrad for the view over the river, lunch in a beer hall, and home through Žižkov under the TV tower with its strange sculpted babies.
people.whyIHost: I photograph my city for a living and I still see something new every morning. Taking somebody along makes me look twice.

people.name: Jana
people.whatWeWillDo: The Saturday farmers market on the river embankment, then the tram up to the castle the slow way. Sunday lunch at mine is svíčková with dumplings, and in the evening, if you like, chamber music in one of the old churches.
people.whyIHost: I played the viola in an orchestra for thirty years and now I finally have time for everything else. Visitors give me an excuse to see Prague as if for the first time.

people.name: Mette
people.whatWeWillDo: We cycle everywhere, so you get a bike for the day: along the canals of Christianshavn, then a cold dip in the harbour with the swimmers who go in all year. After, warm drinks and a long dinner by candlelight, which is what we mean by hygge.
people.whyIHost: I grew up on Funen and came to Copenhagen for university, then stayed for love. Our children are teenagers and embarrassed by everything, so visitors are my best audience now.

people.name: Ravi
people.whatWeWillDo: Nørrebro on foot: the Superkilen park with its objects from sixty countries, then the Assistens cemetery, where Kierkegaard and Hans Christian Andersen lie and locals read on the benches. We end with smørrebrød at mine, made the way my Danish neighbour taught me.
people.whyIHost: I came from Bangalore fifteen years ago for an engineering job and arrived in the dark season with the wrong coat. A colleague took me under his wing, and I owe the city the same favour.

people.name: Keiko
people.whatWeWillDo: Cycling the Tuscan hills for two weeks, with Firenze as my base. I am slow on the climbs and fast at lunch, so I would love a local to show me a market, a kitchen and the quiet streets after the day trippers leave.

people.name: Jun
people.whatWeWillDo: I write about food and coffee and I am in Europe for a month: two weeks in Roma, then Madrid. I want the places your grandmother would approve of, and in return I can tell you everything about Seoul street food.

people.name: Yasmin
people.whatWeWillDo: Architect from Rotterdam, travelling to see how the Nordic cities build homes people actually like. Stockholm first, then Copenhagen: I would love a walk through a real neighbourhood and a coffee in somebody's kitchen.

people.name: Ben
people.whatWeWillDo: Software developer in Europe for two conferences, Paris first and then London. The days are talks and badges; the evenings I would rather spend with a local than in a hotel bar, ideally somewhere with live music.

people.name: Zara
people.whatWeWillDo: Just finished my degree and interrailing on a tight budget: Berlin first, then Prague. I like street art, flea markets and anyone who can show me where students actually eat.

messages.text: Ciao Anna! I got into Milano yesterday by train, with a focaccia from Genova in my bag. Is the Navigli aperitivo still on for tomorrow evening?
Ciao Julien! Tomorrow works, just before I leave for Helsinki. Porta Genova station at 18:30, then we walk along the canal.
Parfait. I bring the focaccia, you choose the bar. And then you tell me what to pack for the north.
Hello Anna, Tom here. I walk into Milano next week, straight down the canal from Lake Como. Is the risotto offer real?
It is real. I am in Helsinki for a few days first and back before you arrive. Come hungry, and bring the walking stories.
Deal. One question first: which football team do I have to pretend to support?
